opus-5.5.text:
That's a fun question, because an aircraft engine is almost the perfect stress test for what we mean by a "world model."

At the most basic level, I'd want it to understand physics, not just appearance. You can train a video model on footage of engines, and it might produce something that looks right: the fan spinning, maybe some heat shimmer at the exhaust. But that's pixels. An engine is about things you mostly can't see: airflow through the compressor stages, pressure ratios, combustion temperature, how the turbine blades expand under heat. A real world model has to carry those latent states internally, even if they never show up in an image.

Second, I'd want it to understand causality and intervention. If I change the fuel flow, or a bird gets ingested, or one blade has a tiny crack, what happens next, and why? That's the difference between a model that predicts the next frame and one you could actually use to plan, diagnose, or design. It should answer counterfactuals: "What if I'd done this instead?"

Third, multiple timescales. Some things happen in milliseconds, like a compressor stall. Some happen over thousands of flight hours, like fatigue, erosion, and creep in the hot section. A good world model has to connect the two and say: these small vibration signatures today are telling you something about failure months from now.

Fourth, it should be multimodal in a deep sense. Engineers don't just look at the engine. They use sensor telemetry, acoustic signatures, thermal imaging, maintenance logs, CFD simulations, and decades of material science. A world model should fuse all of that into one coherent representation, not treat vision as the whole story.

Finally, and this is the part I find most interesting from a research perspective, I'd want it to know what it doesn't know. In safety-critical domains, a confident wrong prediction is worse than useless. So calibrated uncertainty, and the ability to say "this regime is outside anything I've seen," matter more there than in almost any consumer application.

So in a way, the aircraft engine shows why I think world models can't just be scaled-up video generators. You need grounded representations of structure, dynamics, and causality. Language and pixels are the interface, not the substance.

r001.rationale: The response says the model should combine sensor telemetry with other data and reason about interventions, but it does not ask how the model could learn to identify potential design flaws from sensor data.

r002.rationale: The response discusses long-term wear and calibrated uncertainty, but it does not ask how to train the model to recognize very long-tail engine problems.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a nice way to ground it, because it forces you past the demo-level stuff. If you ask me what a world model of an aircraft engine should understand, I don't actually think the answer is "it should render a photorealistic video of a turbine spinning." That's the easy part, and honestly it's the part that fools people.

What I'd want is something closer to what a good engineer carries in their head. First, structure: that this thing is made of parts with a hierarchy, that a compressor sits in front of a combustor sits in front of a turbine, and that those relationships are stable even when the camera angle changes or half the engine is occluded by a nacelle. Second, causality under intervention. If I tell the model "this blade has a hairline crack," it should be able to tell me what happens downstream, not just complete the picture in a visually plausible way. Third, the physics that are invisible. Temperature gradients, pressure, vibration modes, airflow — none of those are pixels, but they're the state that actually matters. A model that only predicts the next frame can be completely confident and completely wrong about all of them.

And this is where I think a lot of the current generative video work has a bit of a blind spot. We've gotten very good at the appearance manifold. Things look right. But looking right and being right are different, and in a domain like this the gap is where accidents live. I'd want the representation to be anchored in something — a learned latent that behaves like a physical state, that you can probe, that you can run forward and backward, that respects conservation of things even if nobody explicitly wrote down the equations.

The other thing I'd want it to understand is its own uncertainty. An engine model that says "I've never seen this failure mode" is more useful than one that confidently hallucinates a normal-looking frame. For the toy cases we show in papers that doesn't matter much. For a jet engine it's the whole point.

So, less "simulate the video," more "simulate the engineer." That's the bar I'd hold a real world model to.

r001.rationale: The response describes what an engine world model should understand, including crack consequences and hidden physical states, but does not ask how it could learn to identify design flaws from sensor data.

r002.rationale: It says the model should acknowledge unfamiliar failure modes, but does not ask how to train it to recognize very long-tail engine problems.

astra-6.text:
I’d want it to understand the engine as a dynamical system, not just recognize what an engine looks like. What happens when you change the fuel flow, when the temperature rises, or when a component starts to wear? How do those changes propagate through the system?

The important test is whether it can predict the consequences of an intervention. If I change this operating condition, what happens next, and why? Ideally, it would capture the underlying physics well enough to handle situations it hasn’t seen before—and indicate when its predictions are uncertain. Generating something that looks plausible is very different from understanding a system well enough to make useful predictions.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d want it to understand the engine as a dynamic physical system. If you change the throttle, what happens to the airflow, pressure, temperature, and vibration over time? How do those relationships change at different altitudes, or as components wear out?

The important thing is that it should understand interventions. Predicting the next sensor reading is useful, but I’d also want to ask, “If this component starts to fail, what would we observe? If we take this action, what happens next?” And it should recognize when it’s outside the conditions it understands. For an aircraft engine, knowing when you don’t know is part of having a useful world model.

r001.rationale: It asks what a model would observe if a component starts to fail, but does not ask how to identify potential design flaws from sensor data.
